utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Assuming that there are no procedural issues, I would like the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just concerned that my case manager wasn't here, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrksic. Please be seated. Mr. Mrksic, a few reminders. First, you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Second, if Mr. Misetic raises his hands, it's not necessarily that he wants you to stop, but perhaps to slow down, and it's not because we don't want to hear your answer. To the contrary, we want to hear your answer, but we need the interpreters for that. So please follow Mr. Misetic and then wait for a while. If he then puts his next question to you, that would mean that you've answered his question. If not, he'll give you a sign that you can continue. Third, if, and I just give an example, Mr. Misetic asks you by what means of transportation you came here, you can just say, I came by car, I came by plane, I came by train. There's no need, at that moment, to tell us what the colour of the car was, whether it was a Fiat or it was a Volkswagen. If he's interested to know about the colour, he'll certainly ask you. So try to keep your answers focused very much on the questions, keep them short. If we need more details, we'll ask you about it. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear, Your Honour. Following the experience I had yesterday, and it was the first time I found myself in such a situation, I suppose I will be able to give answers slowly to everyone's delight, I hope. And I would like to cover all of the ground. I do have a feeling at times that I'm being interrupted at the moment when I'm trying to say something I believe could be helpful both for Misetic and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to find a balance. Let's first focus on the question as it was put to you. It's not criticism. It's just trying to assist and to help you in using our time in this court as efficiently as possible. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask you this: I was given a warning that I shouldn't be talking to this and other person or phone anyone. Am I entitled to give a phone call to my wife and family and inquire if they're well? I don't want to discuss the case. I just want to let them know that I'm feeling well and that I'm in good health. I do understand your instructions, but I haven't been speaking to either the other inmates or my wife, the lawyer is not here, and I'm becoming mute. That's what I -- that's how I understood your warning, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can talk to anyone, as long as it not in any way relates to the fact that you're giving testimony and the substance of your testimony. But if you want to talk about the weather, the food, or your health with your family, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, General Mrksic. Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen again, please, Exhibit D1465, at English page 210. General Mrksic, I'm going to pick up where we left off yesterday, and we're going to go back to this meeting at the end of June in Belgrade about the operation in the Bihac pocket. Now, you see there, towards the middle of the page "JS," whom yesterday you said was Jovica Stanisic, in talking about this operation, and it's page 215 in the B/C/S. If we go down to "JS": "I can find 120 perfect men who would come there in seven days. They would be from the eastern sector - that is support." And then it says: "They should not be engaged ..." And then if we can turn the page please. Then again it says: "JS: Mr. Stanisic, let Mladic arrange it with the 1st and 2nd Krajina corps, and find them to replace the 400 of Pecanac's men and give them to Mrksic. That we form a battalion of volunteers and engage them in ten days - that General Perisic equips them. There are 58, from Kragujevac, Nis, Ljubiskovo." This is the next page in the B/C/S, I understand. Now, General Mrksic, first of all, in preparing this operation, do you recall conversations in Belgrade during these meetings about the transfer of men from, let's say, the command of General Mladic's army and transferring them to your command for purposes of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it being mentioned. But specifically who was supposed to be issued this assignment and what it involved, sending whom to whom, I don't remember. This is the first time I see the mention of Kragujevac, Ljubiskovo. I don't remember that at all. I don't remember at all -- well, this is a piece of paper, an arrangement, and many times, as far as I can remember, such arrangements came to nothing. I can tell you about what I did in Slunj, what I formed in Slunj. I don't remember there being any Pecanac around, I don't know the man, and I couldn't know to begin with because I didn't go to see them over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand. Let me ask you this question: At these meetings, who has the authority to transfer -- you said it was discussed, but you're not sure if it was ever implemented. Who had the authority to transfer men from the Army of the VRS to the Army of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that certain police units were involved, and it was within the competence of the Ministry of Republika Srpska. I am not familiar with their system of command. Normally, the army that was under Mladic's control and command would not come to my -- under my authority. Those must have been MUP or SUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about specifically is the line that says: "Let Mladic arrange it with the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps." The 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps refers to the corps of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: " ... and find men to replace the 400 of Pecanac's men and give them to Mrksic." Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not done. I don't remember it being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Whether it was done or not, my question to you is: Who had the authority to do it, if they were going to do it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- well, I don't know who this person Pecanac was, whether he was from the MUP or the VRS. More likely he was from the MUP. Some other forces were supposed to be found to replace his. The MUP and the VRS controlled the same front-line, just as was the case in the Republic of Croatia. You wouldn't have a situation where the MUP would be holding separate territory from that of the VRS. It must have been regrouping that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is: Who had the authority to subordinate forces of the VRS or of the RS MUP to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been resolved by the president, because the MUP came under the president or the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know who was the minister at the time. They strictly took care to keep their own, and I'm talking about the MUP and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The president of which entity?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, since Pecanac and these forces were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or his minister of the interior, if he authorised him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the next entry says: "Mrksic: Let us pay this corps. Four million came, but I don't know where four is." Can you recall what you were referring to when you said "four million came"?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the conversations that we did not finish that we had in Karadjordjevo. I mean, we did not finish because you interrupted me. Had I told you the entire story, you wouldn't have to put this question to me now. After my appointment as commander, at the meeting in Karadjordjevo I laid out my concept - Mladic was there as well - as to how we should set up the army. I wasn't able to do that merely on the basis of fine words. I needed money for that. The president said, Well, you have Djeletovci there and pumps that work there. Where is this money going to? So they managed to get hold of some funds that enabled me to pay for specialists within the corps at Slunj. I managed to pay out the first salaries, and I transferred the funds to the budgets of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was suddenly revived, thanks to that. Of course, it was the federal organs that authorised the transfer of funds through the SDK, not me. This is nothing to do with the operation. I merely took an opportunity at this meeting to raise this issue. Do you understand now? It has nothing to do with this particular meeting. I merely abused, if you will, the meeting to raise this issue, because he had made this promise to me in Karadjordjevo that he did not follow up on. And I asked, Where's the money, who put the money away?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, eventually after this meeting an operation was undertaken in the Bihac pocket; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the name was "Match" or "Sword," or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether you achieved your objectives in launching that operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a twofold goal, I personally. Well, I was given the assignment, but my aim was to see how these professionals of mine would fare. It was like a drilling exercise to me or a demonstration. There was the entire battalion or a check-point of Polish members of UNPROFOR who admired the professional side of it. I did not want to make this breakthrough in order to incur losses, but rather I wanted to conquer the forces of the 5th Corps. You see, the Pauk command had 10.000 men under their command, and they had expanded their territory. The expansion of the territory was in my favour because I gained depth, which would prove useful in the case the Republic of Croatia refused any sort of peace settlements. I would have this depth where I would be able to protect ordinary people and allow them to pull out. In 1994, we -- at the time when people and the army of Fikret Abdic had fled from the area, we received them, and this was done in World War II as well. I would like you to understand why this balance of power was created. You might not be familiar with this. When there were offensives taking place -- well, you're not allowing me to proceed. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Let me again stress, we want --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's history I'm referring to, but it will not harm anyone. I just wanted to present to you the fact that it was not the whim of the politics of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Always keep a close eye on Mr. Misetic, because he tries to perform two tasks. The first is to slow you down in such a way that we are able to hear what you want to tell us, and, second, to keep your answers within the limits Mr. Misetic thinks is useful for us to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just try to explain something to you, in terms of why it's good if you try to keep your answers focused on my questions. You obviously have a lot of information on every question I can pose to you. I'm aware of that. But from your perspective, the longer answers --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The longer the answers are that give to every question, the longer you're going to be here.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the visit on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Try to keep those answers short and strictly to the question. We will be done faster. Okay. I lost my train of thought now.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me. [Interpretation] That wasn't my intention, to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is: In terms of trying to gain depth, how much depth -- what was the purpose of the operation in terms of how much depth you wanted to gain?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My forces got into the territory -- 2 kilometres into the territory. They crossed the Korana, which was the frontier, and reached the first elevation points near the village of -- and that's where they stopped. They didn't advance any further. This was not the goal. The goal or the objectives were into the depth in the next mountain range, where there were Pauk members present. There I realised that the Dinara was the problem and I aborted this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, I'm not referring just to forces that maybe were under the ARSK command. What was the objective in terms of the depth for the Pauk command, Fikret Abdic's forces and your forces? How far did you want to reach, all three of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignment was not to touch Bihac. Bihac was a protected zone. The instruction was not to irritate the international community. This was a protected area. It was an assignment to the VRS. Another instruction was that towns should not be touched, not even Cazin, which was within range; rather, only the villages which had, through their delegations, spoken their mind to Fikret Abdic in terms of them wanting to cross and go under his authority. I don't know how they settled this issue, what their dealings were. I had only heard that several of the villages had decided to join him. We weren't supposed to go radically and destroy the 5th Corps. Besides, we didn't have the forces to do that. But the corps was in a very bad way, and not because of combat activities, but because marketeering and smuggling activities had been stopped. But we haven't even approached that topic yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Staying on this topic for a minute, if we could go back to Exhibit D923, please, the second-to-last page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, this is that report from the 26th of August sent to the chief of the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army. It's right under the section in the B/C/S that begins under point 19. Now, I'm asking you this in the context of these meetings at the end of June. The second paragraph there under point 19, you write, on the 26th of August: "The Army of the Serbian Krajina was and still is considered a part of the VJ, Yugoslav Army. It was doing everything it could, but it has remained isolated. We think that the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army should have supported development of the Army of the Serbian Krajina in a more courageous and determined way." Now, can you explain that concept of the Army of the Serbian Krajina was and still is considered a part of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that it was the first time I saw the document. The Army of Republika Srpska was an independent body, and it was not merely a branch of the VJ. I wasn't submitting reports to Perisic. I was on equal footing both with him and Mladic. We were three systems. We weren't three united peoples in one state, and there wasn't one person commanding over three front-lines. Simply, they were a brother nation, and I would appeal to them for their assistance in order to make sure that their brethren survived. I didn't write this. These are not my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to what you said earlier today at page 7, lines 22 and 23, when I was asking you about the Operation Match or Sword. Your answer was: "I had a twofold goal, I personally. Well, I was given the assignment, but my aim was to see how these professionals of mine would fare." Now, if you're three separate armies, and you are the chief --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- if you are the chief, the commander of the Main Staff, who is giving you the assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic, the supreme commander, was giving me my assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Martic, who was he receiving his instructions from?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for his instructions, we would have -- those assignments would be discussed by the Supreme Council to assist whether they were in favour or detrimental to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and to see what the objective would gain us. There were general tasks which were imposed by President Milosevic, who was an authority for all Serbian lands. To that effect, we were not, in fact, economically able to do anything without assistance. And assistance to Fikret Abdic was along those lines, in fact, to help the people gain depth, gain the area, where the people could flee if need be, God forbid. And I personally reckoned with 10.000 people, 10.000 combatants of Fikret Abdic. My back was more secure in that case than if I had had a 5th Corps at my command, because Slunj was there in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a different document, General Mrksic. This is Exhibit D953, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 5th Corps behind my back, not at my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you for one clarification of your answer. Page 12, lines 9 and 10, you say: "There were general tasks which were imposed by President Milosevic, who was an authority for all Serb lands." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm looking at your last answer on the transcript at page 12, lines 9 and 10. Ignore the document on the screen for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You answered the last question -- when I asked you who was Martic receiving his instructions from, you answered at page 12, lines 9 and 10: "There are general tasks which were imposed by President Milosevic, who was an authority for all Serbs lands." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, he was an authority, and I admit that because I told you what was the assignment that he had issued me in Karadjordjevo. That is the essence, that is the long-term concept, which was in effect until the fall of the Krajina. And when I spoke about those tasks, my task was for the -- to change the consciousness of the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina by strengthening the army and by joint action and by unity of the MUP and the army, and by annulling some paramilitary units in the villages, in the surrounding area, which would create problems for their commanders, looting, taking away vehicles from UNPROFOR. And my task was to prevent all that and to actually clean up the act of the commanders who would have free lunches and dinners in certain cafes. The leaders would go to the different positions. Television crews would follow them and film their activities. We wanted to achieve unity of the people and the leadership. The aim was to adopt a new position, because we were aware of the fact that we were unable to defend ourselves at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, on this document on the screen at page 2 in the English, this is a report from Mr. Kosta Novakovic, who was an assistant commander of yours; correct? If we could turn the page, please, and --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It's on the first page in the B/C/S now, just so you've seen the note on the bottom. And if we could go back. Now, in speaking of these operations and Operation Sword in Western Bosnia, Mr. Novakovic writes to the Special Units Corps Command, and he says: "Our side, the operations in that area, is presented in the media as inter-Muslim conflicts and is denying the participation of the SVK in these operations, a position we are still holding." Now, why was the SVK denying its role in the operations in the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one shouldn't boast about it. After all, in a way, that was crossing the River Korana to the other side, to the territory, and this involved these divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Republican border, the Republican frontier, was there. This was not characteristic only of us. This is typical of all warfare and of all troops, and this is an excess and one shouldn't actually boast about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, this operation in Western Bosnia, in the Bihac pocket, what was it that caused you to abandon your goals in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We abandoned our goals in that area because, as I learned later through the system, there had been reached an agreement -- some sort of agreement in Split where it was approved to block Western Bosnia, and there was a rapid penetration of HVO forces and Croatian forces from Livanjsko Polje towards Grahovo. So normally every commander is aware of the fact that he will lose his battle, that he will lose everything, if that were to materialise. So I urgently withdrew those forces and sent them there, but I was ordered -- I was requested, and I was already angry by that time, because I wanted to get out with my forces and emerge at Grahovo with my forces and my staff. I wanted to defend that direction from Pejulja [phoen] and onwards, but I received a telegram to the effect, You are prohibited from commanding on our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not find Milovanovic, the general, anywhere. When I went to see Martic to reach an agreement up there, he would flee and no one could find him, he was nowhere to be found. They were dealing with other issues then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And at some point the combined forces of the Croatian Army and the HVO seized Grahovo; correct? You're aware of that? Explain to the Court, from your perspective, what it meant for you when the Croatian Army seized Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that. Thank you for this question. The Republic of the Serbian Krajina, in all its war plans, and you did not allow me to expand on that question, but to tell you what I did when I returned from Karadjordjevo, and if there is time, I would like to expound that so that you will see what happened when Grahovo was conquered. When I perceived the possibilities and the free forces and what my range of action -- what range of action was feasible for me, given my systems, all the towns in Croatia were within my range, I asked the commanders, Why would you open fire that you cannot observe? Prepare your concepts so that you actually engage targets that you can see, because we do not have 10 or 15 rounds of ammunition, but we have somewhere around 0.5. So there was a change of the war plan, in terms of the use of ammunition and pieces, to reinforce the forward end and to rectify all mistakes in engineering works, the breaching of roads, the firing systems improvement, the engineer works, then to change our targets and not to shell settlements and inhabited places, Karlovac, Zagreb, Zadar, and towns which was within range of an M-84 cannon. Next, now I was in position, namely, immediately after returning from Slunj, the operation which I discontinued, I asked the corps commander in Knin, Who is defending Knin for you? He replied, No one, Knin is a free city. And I said, What do you mean, where are your positions? And he said, We never made any positions. The Knin Brigade is defending the area towards Split. And I was amazed, because simply from up there, forces came -- HV forces came, they occupied the firing positions, and they had Knin as in the palm of their hands. In Knin, there were no troops, there were no men, there were just women and children. So I tried to do something with those women, but of course it all came to nothing. When the aggression started, simply prior to the commencement of the aggression, I returned the special units to Slunj to be able to intervene to be able to prevent the lines from being cut off at that direction and near Glina. This was a shock, the arrival of these forces. I went by helicopter to an area below Dinara and tried to see what could be done, together with Commander Martic. We asked for assistance from Republika Srpska, but that was to no avail at all, not to mention the joint meeting of the Supreme Command which took place prior to the very aggression. We didn't know whether it would be the 4th or the 5th. We were expecting the attack, and the attack did happen, it happened on the 4th. It found me in a house in town where I had been relocated, transferred by them. So this is -- actually, my war plan failed, in my eyes. It was a great surprise, but it should not have been a surprise, but it was one because someone let it happen. I will say more about it, if you allow me, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will get into it a little bit, and I want to go back now for one second. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit 65 ter 1D1069, please. Now, this -- if we could go to the signature page, this looks like a document issued by you on the 1st of June, 1995, General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radunovic, Colonel Radunovic. I'd have to read it; I don't know what this is about. And I do not recall this particular Colonel; Radulakovic [phoen], Milan? The chief of the ONO, which is operations and training -- is a general, not a colonel, General Sekulic, in fact. This is not mine. I don't remember this. I don't remember this man. Let's see what it is that he wrote and why you need this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you -- and let's look at point 5 in this document. It says: "Corps commands in their areas shall device civilian protection measures, assign municipal organs and local communes to organise evacuation and accommodation and food supplies for the population (women, children and the elderly) from the potential areas of operations." And then the bottom penultimate paragraph: "Soldiers and the officers of the RSK, we are entering the concluding phase of accomplishing our national aims, and we must not allow any further losses of people or territory. The RSK is more important than the interests and rights of individuals, and that is why I am aware of my responsibility and the measures I am taking." Now, do you recall issuing an order similar to this on or about the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I never issued anything of the kind. That is not my style, and whoever wrote this, and I don't know why they wrote this, really did not deal with local communes or municipalities. This is not my style of expression or of writing, nor is it my document, nor do I know that colonel. But you did not permit me to tell you about everything that I had undertaken and all the measures that I had taken so that you could see what we did. There were things that I organised, but as part of tactical exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You will have plenty of opportunity, General Mrksic, and I'm trying to take this step by step. And, believe me, we will get to everything that we need to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is no document of mine. You can admit it all you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm having problems with my microphone. There we go. I will object to the admission, Mr. President. The witness has clearly not given the foundation for the document, and no foundation exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a document from the Croatian government archives that we received. It goes to probative value and weight. I don't think it goes to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if the witness can't say anything about it, you would tender it from the Bar table as a relevant document; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and since it was put to him here. We can argue it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please mark it for identification and give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1509, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I'd like to show you a video now, and after you've taken a look at this video, I will ask you a few questions about it. Mr. Registrar -- Mr. Registrar, this is Exhibit D136. Transcripts have been given to the booths. This is from RSK Television in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Having heard the sound of sirens, we hurried towards Trzic. It is now five minutes to 6.00. We are located on a bridge crossing the River Mreznica between Trzic and Premizelna [phoen]. We encountered the commander of the 13th Infantry Brigade, Colonel Marko Reljic. As we speak, a column of civilian with vehicles and livestock are arriving from Trzic. What does this mean, commander?" "Well, this is an exercise which we are conducting in accordance with our assumptions, and our information that the enemy aviation will be active in this region, using rockets and artillery. And before this happens we have to evacuate, that is, evacuate the civilian population from the combat area, and our units will complete the tasks that they have been given. That means that it is of importance to us to train the population, the civilian population, to evacuate, as to suffer as little losses as possible." "Are you satisfied with the exercise up to now? Are members of the 13th Infantry Brigade engaged in this exercise, or are they manning their positions?" "Members of the 13th Infantry Brigade are manning their positions, and according to the tasks they have received, all soldiers are at their positions. And I'm very pleased with the conduct of the civilian population. They understand the situation, and they are aware of the fact that we need to prepare and be trained. If we truly find ourselves in a situation we have to evacuate, so that there are no unnecessary victims, so that what happened in Western Slavonia does not happen again, absolutely. "Thank you very much. "You're welcome. "Because Trzic is our first position which will be targeted, so we wanted to test this, and by means of this exercise, we have to review whether we are well prepared, whether we are well organised, and what would be the best way to do this so as to avoid civilian victims, should there be military activity. We need to evacuate the civilian population in due time. After having learned the lesson in Western Slavonia and throughout history in wars, the population needs to be evacuated and removed in time. The units and the army are to remain in their positions, executing their tasks. This is extremely important that you understand, that you know that within your homes and families you need to prepare yourselves, organise yourselves. And upon receipt of the signal, you need to withdraw to the designated region because the enemy wants to slaughter, to murder, to burn, to slaughter these children. That is why every citizen must be prepared for the evacuation. This evacuation won't be signaled in advance. There won't be enough time to prepare. You might have to prepare -- you have to say this, You must be prepared for this."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I -- are you going to put a question to me in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, tell us -- tell the Court why the Army of the ARSK, in July of 1995, is engaged in an evacuation exercise to evacuate civilians. And if you can, in your answer, explain why it was then broadcast on TV Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry. If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was RSK Television, not necessarily Knin Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Let me tell you this: Let me tell you what has been left unsaid so far. We were aware of our position. We know and you know -- take a map and take a look at where Trzic is and where some of our neighbourhoods and villages were along the first line of defence. Under the tactical principles and our rules, and this is something your generals know, the obligations of a commander organising the defence in a certain area is to evacuate the civilian population out of an area which will be subject to direct artillery fire and activity by the enemy, to the left, to the right, in the depth, to remove them from the axis of the attack. There wasn't just one exercise, there were a great many of them, and this individual carried them out in an excellent way. And not only were there these exercises. I wasn't given an opportunity by you to tell you this. When I started organising the army, I was aware of the fact that I would be losing all the communication lines with my subordinates because of the electronic activity and the involvement of NATO, should the aggression take place. We were all hoping it would not. I wanted the commanders to be able to organise independently their defence within their AORs should an attack follow, so that they should be able to launch counter-attacks to engage the forces that were available for counter-attacks, to evacuate the population to avoid great losses. However, I wanted to make sure that no one came out of their AORs, and of course the AORs involved Petrova Mount, a lot of forested land where people could find refuge. This was something that was done during World War II, when the fourth enemy offensive took place involving Ustasha, when they were fleeing their homes to save their lives. So this was not an exercise for the subsequent fleeing in the wake of Storm. This was something quite different. I discussed this with senior officers, security organs, and I talked to different individuals, and I had never heard of anything of the sort. But this was done in an excellent way, and we deliberately broadcast this on TV so as to show how people were getting ready for an all-out war. This was something that we were taught under the concept of the former SFRY. If you want me to add something, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, at the end of the clip, the officer tells the people that, The enemy wants to kill you, the enemy -- these children here will be slaughtered. Now, what is the purpose of telling that to those people and then broadcasting it on television?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps his entire family had perished in World War II, was slaughtered at the time. You know that it was always the population residing there that was victimised the most, and whenever a war topic was broached the idea of throats being cut came up, fears of this and that. Our politicians were responsible for this. Let me tell you that Ante Pavelic's daughter, when she arrived in 1992 in Rijeka, she stated for a novelist that this attitude toward the Serbs was even worse than had been experienced in World War II. The Serbs had this natural fear. I wanted to have a strong army which would enable me to control these fears and compel the international community and the Croatian side to find a way of living together, such as had been found in Eastern Slavonia, but you did not want to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, following up on that point: How did attacking the Bihac pocket contribute to your efforts to finding a way of living together with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't attack Croats in Bihac pocket. We had traded with the Croats in Bihac pocket, cooperated, and worked together along security lines and intelligence. They were our main source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You just told the Court yesterday and today that you were trying to build depth for yourself. You're building depth for yourself against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How -- let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not against; rather, for the defence. I wanted my defence area to be deeper. I could have cut Croatia off and struck a deal with the Slovenians any time, but I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did you think the Croats were going to view your efforts to build depth on the territory of the Bihac pocket, and how did you think that was going to promote your efforts to coexist and find a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for putting this question. This was my line of thinking: If the area where Fikret Abdic was would be expanded, because he was a man of Croatia, he traded across Croatia, and that's how Western Bosnia managed to survive, then tomorrow -- come tomorrow, when coexistence will have been achieved, because you were waging a war with the Muslims in Central Bosnia, you will have -- just as you did have Serbs, you would get Muslims in the Republic of Croatia. You would gain depth, and you wouldn't have the croissant or crescent-shaped country, as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you were launching that offensive to help Croatia expand its territory; you were doing it in Croatian interests?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was doing this so that you would give up on launching an attack, so that we could engage in negotiations, and by gaining us, the Serbs, you would automatically gain something else, the bride, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, let's look and see what happened after Grahovo fell, and let's look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, one thing. Trzic, I think we earlier established for Sector North, is that approximately 40 or 50 kilometres north of Karlovac? Is that -- I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we made a filing on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then I may have forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll check on that during the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 1D1050 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, after the fall of Grahovo, are you -- you're familiar with the fact that a state of war was declared on the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that, but it was abolished very soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who abolished it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Council did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may have lasted for two or three days, because with a state of war, war legislation comes into application. We did not want -- rather, people at large started behaving differently, and we didn't want to have to apply wartime measures and very strict war laws in respect of anyone. It was a problem for me to find someone to fire back at Benkovac, and nobody wanted to go back and defend Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's then not go to this document right away. And based on that last answer, you said: "People at large started behaving differently, and we didn't want to have to apply wartime measures and very strict war laws in respect of anyone."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'm sorry, but Exhibit D939 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, this is from the 29th of July, 1995. Sorry, 30th of July, a decree. If we go to page 2 in the English, it's a proposal by you. Page 4 in the B/C/S, please. Now, this is you writing to the Supreme Defence Council on the 30th of July, 1995, and it says: "Based on the initiative of several corps commands and brigades ... I propose that a decree be issued with legal force on the conditions of the formation and work of the ad hoc military courts, in the case of war or in the case of an immediate threat of war. "These are, in fact, courts-martial. Given that the stated Military Court would try cases of grave criminal offences and that the only penalty is the death penalty, they would be rare in everyday practice and would surely have a great psychological effect on the possible perpetrators. "For this reason, we recommend that our proposal be accepted and that the stated decree be signed by the president of the RSK." Now, General Mrksic, why are you proposing on the 30th of July ad hoc military courts with the power to issue the death penalty?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you quite honestly and candidly, my problem was that the elite had started to flee. When I said "the elite," I meant those who had -- who were loaded, had money, and they were pampered dads -- children. And when people at large see that such individuals fled, then everybody follows their suit. And these individuals, who thought that they were protected for the fact that they were sons of important individuals, I wanted to frighten them. I wanted to enforce law and order. I wanted to send across a clear message that there would be no fleeing tolerated and that they had to stay and fight. Everybody experienced such problems, not just the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why was the elite fleeing to such an extent that you needed to issue -- or request the formation of ad hoc military courts?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had means, they had the wherewithal, they had houses, they had businesses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they stay?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because nobody could prevent them from doing this under the legislation that existed. I wanted to make sure that this way they would be prevented from, and we even erected check-points where they would be stopped, but they still tried to flee across Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think you're understanding my question. What I want to know is, if these people are the elite, if they're the elite --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean the intellectual elite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant professors -- I didn't mean professors and such groups of people. I meant the mob, the mafia men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand. My question is, though: Why didn't they want to stay in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, just because just as your lot, they had links tying them together. They knew one another. They had open channels throughout the war, and they knew what was to happen. They had more information than I did, and of course they were trying to save their skins. The intelligence and business, economic structures, had worked throughout the war. Even today, we have such individuals buying businesses, et cetera. I don't want to have any trouble on account of mentioning them one day when I get released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you know this. You shouldn't have put the question to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question simply is: Were people leaving because they were anticipating that the Croatian Army was going to attack?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that the -- their predictions were that the Serb Army did not stand a chance and could not defend itself; not because that was their opinion, but because they received information from their colleagues, people who engaged in the same sort of activities on the other side. I would kindly ask the President to caution me or warn me if I am going across the bounds of what might prejudice me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is a different kind of prejudice compared to the one we were talking about yesterday. Mr. Misetic is not asking you about names, so therefore, focusing on his question, you don't have to give them, no one is inviting you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't even know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to understand your last answers. Is it that the times of profiteering from the situation appeared to be over once the army would have had to give up the territory? Is that the reason why they left? Is that how I understand your answer? If it's correct, say "yes." If it's not correct, tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Grahovo fell, that was the first indication to them. We were transmitting TV broadcasts to the effect that people should not be leaving, that a solution would be found, that Republika Srpska would be appealed to for assistance, that negotiations might be embarked on, that the presence of UNPROFOR might ensure that this sort of an aggression of that scale would not be launched. We were hopeful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, if we could go back to the document that I had originally put up, which is 65 ter 1D1050, Mr. Registrar. Now, this is an order by you, dated 29 July 1995, and it's to the commander of the Special Units Corps. And it says to: "Urgently group the 2nd Guards Brigade in the area of the village Bruvno, where they are conducting training of the reserve forces of the General Staff of the Serb Krajina Army. Grouping is to be completed on 29 July 1995 until 2000 hours." Now, Bruvno is located where in relation to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you from memory. I don't have a map. It's somewhere there. I can't tell you that without the map. I think it was a training centre. I didn't finish the story about the mobilisations we did in Serbia. I was called by President Milosevic sometime in the month of July, after the 20th of July, and he said to me, Mile, what is it that you're doing? Franjo gave me a call and told me that you were developing some sort of a serious Army there. It's not going to pass just that way, because women's organisations and that sort of organisations started are demonstrating, because they said refugees could not be mobilised. And that's where the mobilisation was stopped. I was sent some 2.400 reservists, and that's where it all ended. We proceeded to perform a serious job. We conducted exercises of an attack, counter-attack, withdrawal, et cetera, just as one would do in peacetime in various barracks. We did not squat down in a shelter, waiting for an attack to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And because of all of that training that you were doing, had you had a few more months, would you have been successful in making that a modern army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been negotiations and there would not have been an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not my question. Had you had a few more months of that training and had you been able, for a few more months, to have all that training, do you think you would have had an army capable of stopping the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Croatia would not have mounted an attack on such an army, because the losses -- no. It was the balance was 6:1, because 400.000 of us could not fight 4 million. That's an absurdity. But we could have inflicted such losses as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, let me try to understand your answer in relation to Mr. Misetic's question. If you would have had a few more months to further train your army, would the balance of military power have been re-established so as that you -- if there ever would have been an attack, that you would have been in a position to resist to such an attack? If it's accurate, say "yes," and if it's not accurate, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would have been able to inflict such losses as would have proved unbearable for the Republic of Croatia. They would have to give up on the idea of an attack and opt for a peace solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, why -- do you recall why are you grouping the units of the Special Units Corps in the Bruvno area on the 29th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall why this was being done in Bruvno, in Lika. Probably an assessment was made to the effect that this proved to be a good area for training or something like that. I don't remember the reason. You know why. The area of Bruvno was quite close to the Knin axis, I believe. I don't have a map, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't want -- I think you may be confusing Brusko with Bruvno, which are two separate places.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Brusko. Do we have a map here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can easily reach the Knin to -- where was my reserve command point? Knin Serb road from Bruvno or, rather, the intersection there. And in this way you could prevent your forces from being cut off and from finding yourself in an encirclement. Probably because of that. It's difficult for me to reconstruct the combinations I had in my mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me give you that map, because that's an interesting point that I wanted to follow up with you on. This is Exhibit P2414, and if you can't -- if the size of the map is not quality enough for you, General Mrksic, I think we may have a hard copy in the courtroom that's bigger. Okay. Now, if we could go to the bottom of this map, please. Now, you see Knin there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I know it's difficult to read the place names, but you see Gracac in the upper middle part?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, from your recollection, the village of Bruvno would be located where in relation to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it must be between Gracac and -- what's this place called to the right of Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Otric.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between Otric and Gracac, or to the north. I'm not sure. I would have to look at the real map. I spent a very short period of time there, and the time I spent there I only dealt with major issues. I didn't visit and see all these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go back now, with the map still on the screen, to your answer at page 33, beginning at line 3. You said: "One can easily reach the Knin to where was my reserve point." And I think we can agree -- everyone in the court can agree that your reserve point was in Srb, which is in the upper --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then you said: " ... or, rather, the intersection there, and in this way you could prevent your forces from being cut off and from finding yourself in an encirclement." Now, can you explain to the Court what you mean by that? How could you have been encircled at that point, and can you tell us which point you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant Knin. With the fall of Bosansko Grahovo and the advancement of forces above Seliste, et cetera. Knin was within range of 120-millimetre artillery as well as all the other types of artillery that were firing upon Knin. And there's something I want to tell you about that as well. The only way out of Knin was the curving, winding road leading toward Otric and Srb, or towards Grahovo, in other words. Towards Otric, because this main road from Grahovo was the main life-line, the supply road, and had been cut off, so it couldn't be counted on. If you controlled the winding road with your fire, nobody could reach Knin, and one could merely walk into an empty town because Knin was not a defended town. If the objective was for the Dalmatia Corps to be disarmed or to be inflicted losses in order to capture the area, then this -- there was no need for this course of action to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm asking you is: Agreed, the Strmica-Grahovo road, you had been cut off there, and is your testimony, then, that if you had to do an evacuation out of Knin, you would have had to go up that road from Knin to Otric and then from Otric to Srb, to your reserve command post; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no -- yes, it was the Supreme Council that issued -- made a decision, and an order was issued. I think you have it there. That was the only solution that we were left with, or to fight in an encirclement at the cost of many human lives, or to evacuate to the territory from Otric to Srb that was under the control of the RSK Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- while we're on this topic, let me jump ahead a little bit and go straight to another order that you issued, because -- to explain this road from Knin to Srb, via Otric. First of all, Mr. President, if I could have that previous document marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1D1050 becomes Exhibit D1510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I don't think there's a reason -- would there be a reason to keep -- no, it's fine. It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could ask everyone to sort of keep this map in their mind, this is Knin-Otric-Srb, and to the left of Otric is a road that goes to Gracac. Okay. And now I would like to show you 65 ter 5954, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, we're going to jump way ahead to the 5th of August, the second day of Operation Storm. I assure you we will talk about the 4th of August in great detail, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll be going back to the first day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. But while we're on this topic, it makes sense that we try to explain topics all at once. Now, this is an order issued by you on the 5th, and it says, the second paragraph: "Excellent results produced in combat operations in the first 15 hours have been jeopardised by such practice," and the practice refers to soldiers and officers leaving their units, "and in some units they have been completely annulled." Now, if we could go to the next page, which is point 1 of the order. Sorry, it's -- yes, point 1.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, 7th Corps. If we could scroll to page 2, there we go, and point 1. And point 1 there, you see that, General, you ordered, "the 7th Corps, with the 103rd Infantry Brigade is stabilising a defence along Mala Dinara-Derala-Otric-Malovan front-lines, by persistent defence with the goal to prevent the enemy taking Knin without being engaged in a battle and joining of the enemy forces which are engaged in directions Knin-Otric, Gracac-Otric, a part of the forces is to continue the battle in the encirclement, one unit is to be sent to the area of Bulina Strana for a defence of the area of Knin and a prevention of the enemy's rapid advance towards Otric." General, which forces of the enemy, the Croatian Army, did you order your forces to prevent their joining and where?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to go through the document fully. Can I look at the document? Is it my document? Yes, very well, fine. Fine, we will go back to it. Go ahead. The gist of it was that from Gracac to Otric, Mr. General Gotovina's forces should be prevented from joining with who it was who was coming from up there, the police or somebody else. Very dangerous forces were coming from up there, across Gracac. For this reason, this particular corps, the Dalmatia Corps, was supposed to regroup. Nobody had been engaging them along the first line of defence. We had been building positions and laying mines in vain, and we only created a problem for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're at a break, but let me ask you one more question on this point. If I understand your answer correctly, you're trying to prevent General Gotovina's forces and the forces of the Special Police attacking through Gracac from linking up at Otric, which would have prevented you from being able to evacuate to Srb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Gracac had already been taken by them, but to prevent them from capturing the territory toward Otric, as you put it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... encircled you and to prevent you from getting out?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to save the people at large. I was trying to do that to save people. The political leadership decided that the people should leave the territory into the depth so that they would not come in harm's way. You're all praising this order, but had this not been done, God knows what the position of the international community and the Republic of Croatia would be today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, we were running short of time there before the break, so I want to follow up with your last answer. And we were talking about the significance of Otric, and you said: "Yes, to save the people at large, I was trying to do that to save people. The political leadership decided that the people should leave the territory into the depth so that they would not come in harm's way. You are all praising this order, but had this not been done, God knows what the position of the international community and the Republic of Croatia would be today." And I wanted to do ask you to clarify what you were referring to when you say "God knows -- had this not been done, God knows what the position of the international community and the Republic of Croatia would be today." What were you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to say, in hindsight and on the basis of all the experiences, and after everything that happened to -- in the wake of Oluja to all the elderly people, to all the people in general who had remained there, imagine now had those forces, those frenzied forces, found all those people there, there would have been great losses, and that would have been to our detriment and to the detriment of the international community. It was a huge area, and I believe that not even the commanders who were in charge of the offensive operations would have been able to control that. We, as a supreme Council, because the president of -- the prime minister, rather, Babic had gone to Belgrade to sign the Z-4 plan, we had the supreme commander Martic and the president of the assembly and some ministers at that meeting, and we took this decision. And I told them, If the people should withdraw, mounting a defence would be a very big problem for us, because these groups all had their families there, everybody would want to protect their own families, and there we would have troubles with that, problems would crop up. But then they decided, although they were aware of the potential for such problems, We are not leaving the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, we are just going into the wooded areas in depth where we can wait for the enemy up front and not from the back. That is why forces were regrouped, that is why such decisions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you ordered the evacuation of the population in order to prevent --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The leaders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the intention was then to form a second front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And where did you want to form that second front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That front-line was supposed to be above Knin, from Gracac, to prevent a penetration from -- towards Srb, a Serbian gate, to meet the enemy face to face. In fact, there were no real fighting. We had no expenditure of ammunition at all. We did not open fire at any targets in depth. We had no one to open fire at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, you had already testified that you did not want Otric to fall, you did not want the forces of General Gotovina and General Markac to link up at Otric because it would have prevented you from --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for them to link up, to prevent the linking up. Had they linked up, the -- or if they had linked up, the defence of Lika and Dalmatia would have been a foregone conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, what would have happened -- what was your assessment at the time, what would have happened if the forces of General Markac and General Gotovina linked up in Otric and your forces were still -- and your forces were still south of that point, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, that is a very good question, because that issue was discussed by the Supreme Defence Council and it was also elaborated through training and demonstration exercises in the corps. But if you'll allow me to time the explain. We had assessments -- we had three or four variants of the possible course that events would take. So if it would happen and we knew that that would happen, mind you, we did not have modern communications systems, so our former JNA systems were over 40 years old, and the fastest connection was by telephone or by railway [as interpreted] but that was only up to Lapac. So we assessed that -- we assessed the method in which the Croatian side would act, the Blues, because we had demonstration exercises, training exercises, as I said, we assessed that they might cut off -- that forces might be cut off and that there would be fighting in encirclement at the corps level, the Kordun Corps, the Banja Corps, in Lika, on that ridge, we would have the Lika Corps towards Lapac, and we were reckoning that the major actions would be directed to Dalmatia from the front and not from Grahovo. There was a change of concept. There was a change of the entire way the fighting was conceived of, and then we saw that we were, in fact, tricked; deceived, that is. So we knew from these other corps what the variants were. Irrespective of the fact whether I would be in contact with them, they were under the obligation to follow the idea, the concept that was actually planned. That is why we had these exercises; the battalion in attack, the battalion in counter-attack, breaching an area, the creation of reserves at brigade level, at corps level. All this was exercised. We were preparing ourselves as in manoeuvres, as in manoeuvring exercises. And when the aggression took place, there was a counter-attack at Karlovac and at Petrinja, and there the -- we inflicted the greatest losses on the attackers, and that was thanks to all the actions that we had exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me get back to my initial question.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say, in the Dalmatia Corps we did not exercise the variant of an aggression from the back. That is why forces had to be moved, and that is why population had to be pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why did it have to be pulled out, why did the population have to be pulled out?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was any squad leader knows of that. If artillery is shelling the forward end and the villages in the forward area, it is the women, the old ladies, and the children that will come to harm, those who are not carrying any rifles, because they can only find shelter in some woods. And this is something which was done in every war. This is an obligation under the Geneva Conventions. Of course, shelling a village is something that should not be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, and we'll talk about shelling, and I will raise issues with you about Vukovar shelling and things like that at a later time. Okay? But let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me get back to my question, which is: What was going to happen, in your view, if, in fact, your forces were encircled at the Otric point?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. Fine, excellent, an excellent question. This is something that I also discussed with the commanders and in a core of the corps, to have fighting in the encirclement and to exert pressure to surrender. It was not the intention -- the objective of the Croatian forces either to have great losses. But in this scenario we foresaw the involvement of the international community which would help avert a massacre or retaliation, and that in that case some of the men who thought that they had done something, that they were guilty of some wrongs, you know, stealing, looting, or anything wrong, that they would leave because they would be afraid of having to appear in court, and that the rest of the people, the ordinary peasants, the ordinary fighters, would be disarmed and return to their homes normally, and that the minority rights would be guaranteed, would have been guaranteed, and not be reduced to just 4 percent, as had been the case in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- let me ask it more bluntly. Did you think that there would be more casualties on your side if, in fact, you were encircled by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it wasn't 1942, when there were no roads. They had roads; they had helicopters. There were also cadaver dogs, and everything could be seen. And great losses would have been inflicted, because of the realistic potentials, the means of destruction and everything, the wherewithal they had, the losses inflicted would have been much greater and everybody would be sorry, those who inflicted them and those on whom they were inflicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I still have this document on the screen from the 5th of August, and I'd ask that it be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1511 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, let me just clarify one comment that you made. You said you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you would allow me, whenever you talk about losses, could you always clearly distinguish in your questions between possible civilian losses and military losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You indicated at page 41, lines 19 to 21, that you weren't expecting attack from the Grahovo side but, rather, from the Dalmatian side and that you were tricked. And could you clarify who tricked you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that was supposed to resolve the issue of Livanjsko Polje, and we had three meetings on that issue and created -- we were to make a plan, but they never had the capacity to actually do it, and they wanted me to do it. Well, General Milovanovic. And who had sent him, he knows that. And that is why I have been carrying this burden for 15 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me take you back to Exhibit D923, if we could have that on the screen again, please. Now, General Mrksic, after the fall of Grahovo, but before Operation Storm, was there an operation planned to take back Bosansko Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an idea was to be discussed and a decision made at the Supreme Defence Council, but it never happened. That was a joint meeting of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in Drvar, but it never materialised. From a position of topographically lower facilities, I had no capacity to ascend against the four brigades of Gotovina against all that artillery located there. My only task was to prevent it from southerly -- from southern incursions into my area. It was a sort of reconnaissance mission that I had. I was amazed that they should be waiting there for three hours, three and a half hours. Why did they not descend down there when it was possible? There was no one there. They could have taken the entire corps captive, and all the people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English of this document. It's page 1 here. I believe it's the fourth paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it says in the middle of that paragraph: "Because of that, a new operation for the liberation of Grahovo was undertaken. The Guards Brigade from the Special Units Corps was transferred to the area of Crvena Zemlja. The two-day combat operations did not better the situation considerably, apart from halting the advancement of the Croatian Army towards Knin via Strmica and towards Licka Kaldrma via the village of Resanovci." Now, do you recall such a two-day combat operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not an operation. These were tactical actions. It is not called an operation. Perhaps wishes were for it to be something -- an undertaking of that scale, but we were aware of what we could do, just to stop it for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operation has a different objective, and this objective was a different one. We liked to use that expression, I mean, to express ourselves at the operative level, operations and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was this operation taking place in the area of Strmica?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The corps commander went there in person to see what they could do. When they saw that they couldn't do anything, it was abandoned. We had over-planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Registrar, if I could have on the screen, please, Exhibit 65 ter 1895, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Misetic, I don't know whether you're going to deal with that, but the exact timing of this operation, which isn't an operation, as I understand, will you pay attention to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let me ask if you recall, General Mrksic, what specific date this --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all this was on the 1st of August, before -- or, rather, I'm not sure when you took Grahovo. On the 28th or the 29th, I immediately transferred a portion of the forces to see what could be done, but it was from Republika Srpska, the territory of the other side, tried to say what could be saved. I read the riot act to the mayor of the city, Why are you not defending the city of Knin, what's happening? And he said, This is a publicly -- he replied, It's a publicly-declared free, open city. No one is going to attack it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I usually do not comment on language used, but if you say "when you took Grahovo," Mr. Misetic did not take Grahovo. He's the one who's examining you. If you wanted to say the Croats took Grahovo or -- it's all fine. Refer to troops rather than to "you," because Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I understand. [Interpretation] I certainly did not mean Mr. Misetic. I meant the Croatian Army and the HVO, certainly, the Sector South that Mr. General was in charge of, was in command of; nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perfect, if you refer to, for example, HV or HVO, so that we know what you're exactly talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who told you that Knin had been declared an open city?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't hold me to my word. I didn't look it up in the Official Gazette. I could not verify that this is the way they tried to bail themselves out. When talking to me, I'm not sure whether that is truth. When I actually lashed out at them, this is what they told me. I know that Knin was the only town in the Serbian Army of Krajina that did not have its own unit. All the others had -- Petrinja had its brigade, Slunj had its brigade, other towns had its brigades. Knin didn't have its own brigade. It was defended, they said, by the Drnis one. So that's the way it was. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
