utterances.text: Well, that is it. That is what I was talking about. I have already talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: About preventing families and members of --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. They saw the well-off ones leaving, so some officers started sending of their families and children in a clandestine manner. So I told them, Look at the people, see what you are doing. What do you think they will thinking about -- what do you think they will think about us? So I forbid this. This is correct, what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, I tender -- I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1512.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D1465 again on the screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, do you recall having a meeting with Ratko Mladic in Knin on the 30th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I had no meeting, no such meeting. That is a mistake. That is why that I believe this diary, this log-book, was written in hindsight, and I cannot accept that. I did hear that he was with the patriarch, but I was in Slunj. I never saw Mladic. When we were supposed to resolve the question of Livanjsko Polje and the features on Dinara, nobody was able to get hold of him. I was unable to establish contact with him. He was not with me, and this is incorrect information. And on the basis of this incorrect information, I actually have doubts about everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question, General: If General Mladic was in Knin, meeting with members of the ARSK Main Staff, given the fact that you were -- if he were, why would he be talking to members of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not talking -- he did not talk to members of the Main Staff. This is something the media concocted, because earlier he served in Knin and was attached to the people there. And now he spoke on television, I don't know why. Had I been there then, I would have told him everything that I have told you about the fall of Grahovo and everything else, and then quite a conflict would have erupted then between the two of us because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never actually acknowledged any authority, including that of Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is page 239 in the English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are mere assumptions, all these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and page 244 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, how were you aware that Mr. Mladic appeared on television in Knin when he was there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosta Novakovic, the commissar, commissar, told me that he had come there and asked to appear on television, a press conference. I'm not quite sure what it was, but I know what his style is. He likes that, he likes to speak in public. I was not there, so I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So now if you look at the screen here, and Mr. Mladic's diary, it's 30 July 1995 from 1600 to 1700 hours: "Knin. Meeting with the Main Staff of the Serbian Krajina Army." You're saying you have no knowledge of such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Mr. President. I believe the witness's testimony was that there was no meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No meeting at all, nor did he have any authority to hold a meeting with my staff. He could have asked them about how they were and things like that. It was only me that could have -- that could hold a meeting with my staff. Now, what he did, why he hadn't sent word to me that he would be coming, that is a quite different matter, and that is all hindsight, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, you said you were in Slunj on that day. Whether somebody met with someone from the ARSK Main Staff or not, you wouldn't know if you were in Slunj. And you acknowledge that he was in Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Knin. I was told that he arrived there and gave statements of sorts. I wasn't there. I was dealing with vital issues. Had he sent word to me that he was coming to Knin, I would have gone there. That's why I don't accept this as being any sort of meeting. It was his private visit, and he obviously brought the patriarch along. What his reasons were, I don't know, dragging an old man down there. Probably he had a reason of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, let me turn your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's get this clear. Nobody can command the Main Staff, save myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I didn't suggest that Mr. Mladic was commanding your Main Staff, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think you let yourself go. The whole line of questioning, a meeting with the Main Staff, would that mean the complete Main Staff? If you're in Slunj, you might not know, but -- unless all the members of the Main Staff are with you there, so it's a rather complex matter which is not that easily dealt with. Apparently, the witness, from what I understand, that you have knowledge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half of the command was with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the other members of the command were where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half of it was with me at the IKM in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commissar, the commissioner, was down there, and I don't know if anybody else, I mean in addition to Kosta Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were not informed of them meeting with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even the president of the republic was there. I was informed of it subsequently by phone and when I got there later on, but there was no declarative statement to the effect that they would be doing this and that by way of providing assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you exclude for the possibility that members of the Main Staff that were Knin may have met or may have had a conversation with General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An informal conversation, perhaps, in passing, because they knew each other from 1991 or 1992, when he was serving there, and he knew quite a few of the officers there. But no official meetings or talks could have been held, since I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, I want to turn your attention to 65 ter 1D1074. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read through it. It's a very poor copy. There is no date. When does the document date from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we look -- if you turn the page and look to the bottom, all the way to the bottom, you see somebody wrote in hand a date with a number.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 31st of July. Can I now read through the document? Can we have the top of it? This is precisely the way things happened, the way this assessment outlines. Can we go to the bottom of the page? Back a bit. Can you -- can we go up? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this an order that you issued, to the best that you can recollect?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the orders given, it does seem logical. I can't tell you whether I issued the order. It's not the signature that matters; the contents do. I don't know what it is you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, point 5 in this document, if we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me read it out in English. A portion of point 5 says: "All the population that has not been assigned anywhere should be put into military territorial units." Can you explain what the purpose of that portion of the order is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military territorial units were units of -- that were governed by work obligation. I realised that Knin had not organised anything in terms of its defence in the direction of Dalmatia, as if it was Belgrade and not Knin. These units were tasked with assisting the population. It consisted of elderly people, like the village guards that existed in 1991 or 1992. Women and men together were supposed to go and build shelters, and that's only logical. Any commander would order that. I see my counsel has arrived. Welcome, Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just follow up, and then we can deal with whatever procedural issues the Chamber wishes to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "However, these elderly women and" -- I'm sorry: "These units consisted of elderly people." These elderly people, according to this provision, were put into military territorial units, though.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I read this out. I was telling you this from my memory. I don't know what it is that the document says. The copy is very poor. But I do believe that what I told you should be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit, marked, and I tender this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Just for the record, could you introduce yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honours, Vladimir Domazet, counsel for Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Domazet, you have been invited to come to The Hague because Mr. Mrksic expressed a strong preference for counsel to be present in court with him when he gives his testimony. We, nevertheless, started yesterday without any counsel being present. The matter may have been clear for quite a while, that the Gotovina Defence intended to call Mr. Mrksic as a witness. The Chamber has been informed about communication between Mr. Mrksic's counsel, at least counsel at the time - I do not know whether you consider yourself still to be counsel of Mr. Mrksic - where he has been convicted and sentenced finally by the Appeals Chamber. Being aware of these serious attempts to keep you updated on the moves the Gotovina Defence intended to make, the Chamber was not struck by the communicative skills or at least what happened in this communication. Now, that's the reason why this Chamber decided yesterday that Mr. Mrksic had had every opportunity to address the Chamber and you would have had every opportunity to address the Chamber on the matter. At the same time, the Chamber wished to assist Mr. Mrksic to testify in the presence of counsel. The Chamber clearly expressed that there is no right for a witness to be assisted by counsel. At the same time, it is not uncommon that someone testifies in the presence of counsel. Now, the role of counsel in this respect is rather limited. I take it that you understand that. That means that no advice whatsoever can be given on the substance of the testimony. It's very clear that the only thing a witness has to do is to answer the questions in accordance with the truth and to his best recollection. Before we started yesterday, I informed Mr. Mrksic about his duty to testify; that not answering questions would possibly expose him to further investigation and prosecution for contempt of court under Rule 77. I also informed Mr. Mrksic about the contents of Rule 90(E), which protects a witness to self-incrimination, and also the powers of the Chamber to compel a witness, nevertheless, to give answers. We have -- you can find that on the record, that we have dealt with all those matters. I think that the role of counsel in this respect is limited to those matters; that is, not the substance of the testimony, but rather of the position of a witness, the duties of a witness, and the rights of a witness. If you'd like to make any observations, if you would have any questions in relation to this, you're invited to bring them to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am familiar with the

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: (redacted) However, at the time I received timely notice from the Registrar. I had enough time to meet with the witness or, rather, my client. Unfortunately, this time it was not possible, although my colleague, Mr. Vasic, who was lead counsel to Mr. Mrksic, was in touch. I saw him yesterday in Belgrade, and he told me that he had expected the Registry to inform him of this appointment. However, both the subpoena and the summons arrived far too late for him to obtain a visa. At any rate, we agreed that I would follow the proceedings. I followed the proceedings fully over the internet yesterday, but nevertheless I should like to be provided with the transcripts of both the session yesterday and the session this morning, which I was unable to attend due to my travel by plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I take it that there will be a possibility to provide Mr. Domazet with a hard copy of the transcript once it has been finalised? Perhaps even an electronic copy could be made available to him, if it's not yet finalised. As far as your role is concerned, there are no further questions, no further submissions, Mr. Domazet? You said, Well, we would have expected to be invited. Well, it is for a witness to express that he wants to have counsel present in court. Never anything of the kind reached this Chamber. And I think that if you would have responded to the earlier attempts to contact you by saying, Well, feel free to call whatever witness you want, if it would be Mr. Mrksic, please be aware that -- inform us about it well in time so that we can address the Chamber, or, We inform you that I would like to be present during the testimony of Mr. Mrksic, would that meet any objection, then I think which a more communicative approach, the matters might not have taken the course they have taken. If there's anything you'd like to respond to that, because these might be a bit harsh words, you have an opportunity to do so. If you, however, suggest that we just proceed, we'll do so as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just explained that I wasn't part of the communication, it was Mr. Vasic. And if there had been some omissions on our part previously, there are none now, and we can proceed just as you said we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to give you a fair chance to respond to my words. We can proceed. Mr. Misetic, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit 65 ter 1D1051 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, this is not your order. This is an order of the General Staff of the Serb Army of Krajina, issued by Major General Loncar on the 1st of August. If you could take a look at that, and you see in paragraph 1, he says: "Commanding officers of departments, sections, and organs of the General Staff of the Serb Krajina Army shall, within their authority, carry out preparation of means and documentation for relocation. In the course of the preparation, sort and pack the documentation according to that which is going to be taken to the new location and that which is to be destroyed. The destroying is to follow after the decision on the relocation of the General Staff of the Serb Krajina Army." And then if we go to -- there's several other components of the order, but if we go to page 3, paragraph 10: "All preparations for the relocation are to be carried out immediately. Readiness for all tasks and obligations regarding the relocation of the General Staff of the Serb Krajina Army on 3 August 1995 until 2000 hours, when the organs' commanding officers shall report on the readiness status." Now, my question, General Mrksic, is: Why would the General Staff, as of the 1st of August, be preparing to relocate or destroy documents of the SVK General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a purely military matter. Since the assessment was that an aggression was imminent, whether it was going to be on the 4th, 5th, or 6th, none of the commands or staffs remain as they were. They have to be divided into the main command post and rear command post. Otherwise, one would be able to destroy the staff with a single blow, just as you did on the 4th in the morning, you struck the location of the Main Staff. And that's the proper procedure of relocating matters. You do not take along matters relating to the peacetime, which only consist of burden, they have to be jettisoned, they have to be destroyed, and this is done pursuant to an order of the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff left with part of the command, and I stayed behind in Knin with the other part of the command and with the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- you say now that this was done because you were anticipating the attack. The paragraph 10 seems to provide pretty accurate information about when the attack would take place. Why didn't you just move your entire command out of Knin to the forward command post or to your reserve command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just quickly -- just a question on what forward command post Mr. Misetic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He mentioned it in his last answer. He said the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: He said main and rear command post. I'm wasn't sure if there is a distinction between where he was and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it. It seems not -- if that would assist Mr. Russo, the quickest way of doing it, Mr. Misetic, is to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I was listening to him in the original, so let me ask him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many command posts did you say you had, you were preparing?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the main reserve command post and rear command post. That's the case with all the armies, including the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I -- correct me if I'm wrong, but I thought I heard you say "IZM."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- yes. Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought I heard you say "IZM." Maybe I misheard you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rear logistic command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, the same question, essentially. Why didn't you move the entire command out of Knin to the rear command post?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me answer this. In a war, where one expects an attack, an act of aggression, five to ten days ahead of the aggression at any time in a timely manner, the units have to be dispersed, command posts have to be dispersed. One should not wait for the first blow, because that's the most lethal one. That would be equal to murder, for a staff to remain headquartered where it was, waiting for an attack. It would be a move on the part of a dilettante, rather than a professional general who had done his schooling. That's how it is. Where an attack is anticipated, the command has to be divided into three structures; the reserve command post, where the commander would be; the reserve command post, where the Chief of Staff was; and the logistics post, where the chief of logistics is. Where the command post is destroyed, then the reserve command post or the rear command post would become the main command post. There can be no situation where an army does not know where its command post is or where the organ in charge of combat activities is situated. That's your textbook knowledge of warfare. They went to Srb, if that's what you'd like to know, where the reserve command post was stationed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, information reached me that a forward command post in Croatian might be "IZM," whereas in Serbian it might be "IKM," so therefore this might be one of the occasions where the differences between the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... play a role. It's not my own knowledge. I had that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one second, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same terminology was used before, when they went to the same schools I did. They are familiar with that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the matter has been sufficiently clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just find the portion of one of your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So in terms of the purpose of this order, were you, in fact -- in terms of preparing to relocate the Main Staff, were you anticipating that the Croatian Army would attack the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intelligence services were working non-stop. They were constantly in touch with your lot there. They were crossing over to each side, back and forth. I knew where each battalion was heading. But that was not the point. The point was that I was unable to prevent the attack. That's how strong they were. In other words, we knew that the attack was imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Croatian Army would target the Main Staff building?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's task number 1 of every soldier, to strike at the Main Staff. If I were a gunner, I'd be shooting only at that and nothing else, only the Main Staff. And let me tell you now that you've raised the matter, if the Court allows me to, we will have to tell this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Now, it goes back -- now let me go back. If, as you say, if you were a gunner, you'd be shooting at only that --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question again is: Did you ever consider, given the location of the Main Staff in the town, to move your command out of a populated area and to go to your rear command post?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander does not go to the rear command post, but to the reserve or alternate command post. But the Chief of Staff went to the reserve command post, and they stayed there. How would the people feel if the entire command were to flee? I'm asking you. Knin was full of people, women, and children, and the command has fled? I didn't want to leave my command post. I sent the commander with us to be able to command from up there. If something should happen to me, I would remain there with the president of the Assembly with the minister in our command post in the basement, and they remained in my office. However, I did not spend that night at the command post due to some reasons; namely, my security staff, my intelligence services, actually told me that if I remained there, I would be bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, finally, while we're talking about your security staff, your intelligence services: Paragraph 10, how did you get that information, to be ready by the 3rd of August at 2000? Do you know how that intelligence was obtained?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of August was when the command post was supposed to be relocated. And as for the attack, all the anticipation was it would be on the 4th and possibly on the 5th. The forces of General Gotovina were above Knin, and they were observing all our activities via binoculars, so we were expecting an attack. Plus all the intelligence and information that was coming in from all quarters obviously said that there was an attack being prepared. Actually, in cooperation with all the political organs, with all my corps, I tried to force the politicians and all these leaders to opt for a peaceful solution, as was my plan, but that didn't materialise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please slow down for the benefit of one and all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, again you are invited to adopt a different speed of speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. You know, I've been burdened with this onus, a difficult psychological burden, for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not that we have no understanding, but nevertheless we would like to hear your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And my arms are starting to hurt from trying to slow you down, so if we could -- thank you, General. Mr. Registrar, if I could have the exhibit on the screen marked -- or, Mr. President, if I could have the exhibit on the screen marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have, please, 65 ter number 1D1052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, this is an order issued by you on the 2nd of August; and it's a decision on further combat operations; order. Now, it's a lengthy document, so let me go through it with you step by step.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to read it through to see what it is about, if you will allow me. I haven't seen this document in perhaps 15 years. Perhaps I didn't even draw it up and perhaps I wrote it in haste. And I'm not sure if that is the case, what I wrote, so I have to read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would give the witness a hard copy of the original. Perhaps it will be faster for him to review it on paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes, yes, please. [Interpretation] Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And does that look like an order that you issued on the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And after that, I was not able to issue any other orders because the communications did not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We're going to continue on with this document, but I want to clarify something that you answered earlier by showing you a new document. Remember, we discussed Mr. Mladic being in Knin, and you said you were in Slunj. Do you remember, on that exact date, you attending a meeting with Mr. Martic and --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember being present in Knin on that very day with Mr. Martic meeting with Yasushi Akashi?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I was at all meetings with the president precisely on account of all the tasks I was given after the meeting in Karadjordjevo, and that we were to advance a joint position before representatives of the international community. Now, as for that particular day, I don't know. What I do know is that I was not with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can via Sanction, show a memo prepared by Mr. Akashi about his visit to Knin on the 30th of July, and we will tender the document later. The 65 ter number is 1D1586, and we're showing it via Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't have a translated copy, so you'll just have to listen, or I know you speak some English, so if you can follow along. This is Mr. Akashi's memorandum to Mr. Kofi Annan. The memo is dated the 1st of August, but in the first paragraph you'll see, he's reporting on: "The results of my meeting in Knin on 30th of July." And paragraph 2 in the middle, he says: "I was accompanied in the meeting by the force commander and senior aides. President Martic, dressed in a camouflage T-shirt, led the delegation from Knin and was accompanied by General Mrksic." Does that refresh your recollection about a meeting that you attended with Yasushi Akashi in Knin on the 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were at meetings many times, and I sought that I was always present at such meetings, because representatives of the international community insisted that I do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can go back to the document in e-court. The order that you have now in front of you on paper, this is your decision on an order on further combat operations. And in the first paragraph, you say: "The territorial integrity of the RSK has been jeopardised by combat operations of the Croatian Army from the Dinara ridge and from Grahovo towards Strmica and Knin." Now, you say -- I'm sorry, and if we can look -- let's look at the sentence before that. In that very first paragraph, you say: "It is expected that the aggression might be initiated with the main forces on the axis Plaski-Slunj-Sturlic and with a part of the forces on the axis Sunja-Kostajnica - valley of the River Una." Now, those places in that sentence, Plaski, Slunj, Sturlic, are areas in Sector North; correct? Yes? You have to speak.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still listening to the interpretation. Yes. What is the problem there? These are the precise assessments that we had, and it was the most logical variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going back to that second paragraph, you talk about the combat operations Grahovo-Strmica-Knin: "Several demonstrational attacks can be expected aimed at achieving surprise and concealing the axes of aggression." And then you say: "Count on the Croatian Army using air-strikes on the axes of combat operations by the main forces, but also fake strikes at favourable areas in order to create confusion." Now, if I read that correctly, you anticipated the main attack would come in Sector North and that the -- from the direction of Grahovo would be demonstrational or fake strikes aimed at creating confusion and masking the true aim of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually thought that the main attack would come from Grahovo and through Grahovo, and that was our major problem. Our earlier assessment, or war plan, was based on what you have just said, Strmica, the linking up of the 5th Corps with the forces from Ogulin, the nearest part, and near Glina from Stankovac to Glina and then linking again up with Western Bosnia, and of course normally down there by Slunj, cutting off the direction towards Republika Srpska. Those were our assessments. Actually, according -- everything evolved according to assessments, except that we did not assess and anticipate that we would be attacked from the back. And we even assessed all the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to section -- the paragraph B, okay, it says: "The attack on the units which prepared the areas in defence positions are preceded by several hours or days of artillery fire. The artillery inflicts losses, evokes fear, and is aimed at trying to lead the soldiers to abandon their positions for defence prior to the attack itself. The largest psychological effect the Ustasha have been accomplishing by using multiple rocket-launchers. The precision was more weak than well. The Ustasha started the attack only if the soldiers afraid from the artillery fire would leave their positions without a fight." So you were anticipating that the Croatian Army would use -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] More correct writing, missed the writing totally correct. [Interpretation] It wasn't read correctly, what was written. Multiple rocket-launchers, these are not mortar and these are not just launchers, this is a huge difference, like chalk and cheese. You didn't do it deliberately, I'm sure. Perhaps it is just that you lack military training. The greater psychological effect was achieved by Ustasha by actually using multiple rocket-launchers -- the precision was weak rather than good. The Ustasha started the attack. Only the soldiers were too afraid from artillery fire would leave their positions without a fight, and that is quite logical. This is something that I, myself, would have done in such a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go to paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under C?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, paragraph number 2, after paragraph D: "All SVK units are at the highest level of combat readiness. Combat operations are in progress, with a part of the forces on the Dinara ridge and the defence of the Grahovo-Strmica axis." And it says: "After losing Grahovo and Glamoc, the 2nd Krajina Corps is rapidly conducting engineering work on positions for the defence of the Grahovo-Drvar axis." And now this sentence: "New forces are being rapidly brought in from depth and prepared for conducting a counter-attack on HV/HVO forces on the Grahovo-Livno access and the Glamoc-Livno axis. In paragraph 4: "I have decided by carrying out --"

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a bit peculiar, a bit strange. This is a neighbouring adjacent structure; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the commanding methodology? What is the adjacent unit doing, what is the neighbouring structure doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: In paragraph 4, what you decided is to carry out a persistent defence to slow down and prevent a possible attack --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extreme -- extreme and persistent defence. This is the last-ditch defence, decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... decisive defence, to slow down and prevent a possible attack by the HV on the chosen axes, while simultaneously carrying out an operation to liberate the Knin-Grahovo-Drvar communication and take control of the Dinara ridge, with the purpose of creating conditions for a more favourable treatment towards RSK's interests in the negotiating process which has started." Now, if I understand this correctly, General, what you intended to do was mount a defence against what you thought were going to be the Croatian Army's main axes of attack and simultaneously conduct your own --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, against Mr. Gotovina, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your plan was to launch a counter-attack to take Grahovo back while the Croatian Army was attacking --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot mount a counter-attack against such forces. I just wanted to slow them down. I'm sorry, I apologise. So the objective was to halt them on the most important axis which was endangering the capital city, which was undefended, practically. Because delegations had left with the empowerment, with the authority to sign whatever was necessary. They had gone to Geneva. Martic had ordered the prime minister to go to the American Embassy and to sign the Z-4, and I was also supposed to go, but the late Mr. Cervenko was not supposed -- was not willing to receive me. I was to go to Turanj with him and to accept everything that Mr. Cervenko asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- again, as I understand the document, paragraph 1 talks about the main axes of attack being the areas that you've said are in Sector North, and the language in paragraph 3 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And paragraph 4, you talk about carrying out an operation to liberate the Knin-Grahovo-Drvar communication. An operation to liberate that communication would involve an offensive operation, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, sir, you skipped over paragraph 3, because we had information from the neighbours, from Republika Srpska, that they were pulling in forces and mounting offensive actions towards Grahovo from Drvar. And I, as the endangered side, had to follow my concept. So this is the conceptual part of the decision, item 4, that I was also to participate in making this road passable, if breaching this communication, if you understand me. But these were -- you know, this was more wishful-thinking type of decisions. They were not backed materially, but the decision -- because the decision has to be backed by equipment, and technical and materiel equipment. This pulling in of forces from Eastern Bosnia, this took days. By that time, Knin had fallen, half of Krajina had fallen, and all of Krajina had fallen, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm looking at the clock. It might be time for a break, unless you have one or two questions which would conclude a certain chapter or a certain subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to complete this document, Mr. President. I have one question left on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a short document. If you can do that in a couple of minutes, fine, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, we can take a break now. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, could I turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We have a break, and we resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, perhaps I should address you, Mr. Waespi. There was an informal request by the Cermak Defence for exceeding the word limit in the sur-reply on the matter of Rule 68 disclosure. Is that a matter on which you would like to respond or, knowing the Cermak Defence, that they usually are rather succinct --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll leave it in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the request is granted, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, while we still have this document on the screen, I believe it's -- if we go to page 3 in the English, paragraph 5, which in the original -- the original starts: "The KSJ, not including the 2nd pbr ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your order, you said: "The KSJ, not including the 2nd pbr and went with the 75th mabr, parts of the forces from the 21st Corps and Pauk are deployed in the waiting area of Slunj - village of Brocanac - Batnoga on readiness for a counter-attack ..." Now, why did you deploy -- this Special Unit Corps was --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't read it well. Can I explain, then, read this out, just to assist you? The Special Units Corps, without the 2nd Guards Brigade, with the 75th Mixed Artillery Brigade, mbr, these are 130-millimetre guns from the 21st Corps, and the Pauk units or, rather, Fikret Abdic's units deployed in the area, the waiting area Slunj, village of Brocanac-Batnoga, be at for readiness for a counter-attack in the direction of Glina. It was our intention that via Kladusa, they would be linking up through Glina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I have some problems with what appears in the original and what appears on the -- on our screens. Apparently, paragraph 5, which has a heading, is subdivided in various paragraphs in the original, whereas what we see at this moment is a paragraph 5 without heading and appears to be something -- perhaps it's the subparagraph, what we see left and right is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Now we have it right on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead and finish your answer, General.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reserve forces, in other words, my forces, the forces of the commander of the Supreme Staff, that's to say Matic, they were there in case an aggression was launched to engage in active combat along the axis that might possibly be threatened. And then the Slunj-Rakovica road, I don't know why it is was that we assumed that the Croatian forces would have some sort of landing operations. We were, obviously, fearful of them. The axis of active combat should be coordinated with the Banja and the Kordun Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Understood. And what you're talking about is you're not sure why you assume the Croatian forces would have some sort of landing operations up in Sector North; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there were none, there were no landing operations, but obviously somebody fed this information to our intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That it was going to be up in Sector North; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believed that that was the best area for Croatian Army to cut off the Banja and Kordun from Lika and Dalmatia Corps. I didn't count on what would subsequently happen with Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of what you anticipated happening from behind you, from Grahovo, did you -- did you anticipate that the main action of the Croatian Army from Grahovo would be via the Grahovo-Strmica-Knin road?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I anticipated that the thrust of the attack would be on the road above Knin. Knin, itself, was undefended. I anticipated that the forces of the HV and HVO would be launching a landing operation there. That's why I kept the unit you asked me about close to that location. What's it called? Not Obrovac; Potok or Otisic [phoen]. Bruvno, right. That's why I kept the reserve forces there, because I was afraid of them cutting off the corps and encircling it. We were going through these various scenarios of finding ourselves in encirclement. However, it appeared then that they were not interested in encircling us. They were merely shelling from down there. And as the population was returned, they advanced. That's why I was surprised by, their manner of advancement. They caught me by surprise there 100 percent. As for the other axes covered by the Banja and Kordun Corps, all these developments kind of followed the logic that we were preparing for in our exercises. However, we did not anticipate what the southern flank of the Croatian Army, under the command of General Gotovina, would be doing. That's why I had my mates who helped me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1515.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, there came a point in time that you replaced the commander of the 7th Krajina Corps, Kozomara, with Mr. Kovacevic. Can you tell us, first, when you did that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozomara, yes. That was shortly before the attack, roughly at the time when the fighting was going on around Grahovo. Kozomara did not prove to be resourceful. He did not -- he wasn't able to use the sources that were there defending Benkovac and elsewhere, where there was no threat, in fact. He should have regrouped those forces and used them where they were needed. He was a good officer. However, apparently he was not in a good psychological state. He was not in a good state of mind, since he, himself, asked for another individual to replace him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this wasn't the only poor psychological state that we had. I had my subordinate who committed suicide. These people were made of flesh and blood. He was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, where did Mr. Kovacevic come from? From what post was he promoted to the position of the commander of the 7th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kovacevic was chief of armoured units. Since I used to work in the land forces before, I was chief of the land forces -- let me explain this. He, as a Serb volunteer, having seen what the situation was like there, he volunteered to go there on his annual leave. He wasn't dispatched there by the General Staff. They even forbade officers to cross the Drina on their way there, but there were others arriving as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was the impact of me being the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record -- just so the record is clear, General Kovacevic was an officer in the Yugoslav Army -- a general in the Yugoslav Army who then replaced Mr. Kozomara?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Kozomara stayed behind to work with him, but he took charge of everything because he was a stable person, and he personally took it upon himself to take care of the positions up on the Dinara. The other ones didn't dare show their noses up there; not because they were afraid, but because they had been engaged in the war for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention back to D1495. Sorry, 1465. I apologise. Page 240 in the English, and page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 240 in the English and page 245 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, do you recall going to Drvar on the 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were Mr. -- were you present at that meeting with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Ms. Plavsic, as well as General Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- Milovanovic, Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting of two supreme commands. It was supposed to be a meeting, but it did not turn out to be one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the purpose of you all getting together on the 2nd of August in Drvar?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to resolve the issue of pulling out the breakthrough and causing the fall of Grahovo, et cetera, and the arming of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. This was the purpose of the joint meeting. Mladic and I, chiefs of staff, were supposed to submit reports, and the commands were supposed to take decisions, What do we do next? We had water up to our chins. Now, what happened? There was no meeting. There ensued a quarrel in the leadership of the Army of Republika Srpska, between Mladic and Krajisnik, or, rather, Karadzic. And all at once NATO aviation appeared. I told Matic, Let's go back, this is to no avail, let's save our skins. So that's how it ended. I don't trust anything that's put on paper here, because this is not the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you look at this paper and see, in terms of the names there, do you recall all of those people being present?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall all of them. I know about Martic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, who approached me and told me, Good for you, you are so unified. Why don't we have such a unified leadership? That's what I remember. Probably Tomanovic, the commander of the corps, was there. And as far as I remember, Milovanovic was there, since he was in charge of the entire area as of the month of June. However, there was some sort of an excess there when we entered the meeting room, some sort of a quarrel, and then the aviation appeared, and that was the end of the story; no discussion, no conclusions. I didn't even get to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, earlier, when we looked at the previous -- your order from the 2nd of August, which was the last document we looked at, you indicated that, in fact, part of your order reflects that the 2nd Krajina Corps, which was under General Mladic's command, was supposed to launch an offensive operation against General Gotovina's forces in Grahovo when the Croatian offensive began; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Information was received along the communication lines between the staffs. This was their plan which was materialised who knows when. But this was not the subject of this particular meeting of the two supreme commands of two countries, the Republika Srpska and the RSK. Perhaps it would have been, had not this altercation or verbal conflict emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In terms of your previous order, which was issued on the same day as this meeting, was there some agreement or understanding between you and General Mladic that you would defend and General Mladic's forces would attack? Otherwise, how did you know --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Staffs received information to the effect of what the adjacent units were doing, what the adjacent corps were doing, and our adjacent corps was the Krajina Corps, and they reported on all the areas where they broke through. They said that they would launch an offensive and that we would be doing the same from the other side. General Kovacevic, whom you mentioned, had a company -- we didn't have forces. Everything was tied up along the front-line, along the depth of the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned General Kovacevic. Where was General Kovacevic's command located once he took over the 7th Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the barracks in town, the Northern Barracks, and somewhere in Strmica. He relocated later on, and then subsequently he was at the railway station in Knin, and that's where he supervised the pulling out of the forces. And he was the one who was covering the back for the IKM in Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, General Kovacevic, as the commander of the 7th Krajina Corps, his command was located in the Northern Barracks at first; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until combat activities commenced. When they did, just as my command did, he got up -- got out to the railway station and perhaps towards Strmica, at the IKM there, because he was practically on the slopes of the Dinara with some elements of his army. That's where the IKM was, and the command post was up at the abandoned railway station. I don't know what it's called, the one above Knin. That's where we found him that night. Martic stayed the night there. We spent nights there, and he stayed behind at the corps, had a nap for perhaps two hours, and I continued my journey to Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to this meeting in Drvar, do you recall a discussion at that meeting in Drvar on the 2nd of August about the people of Grahovo and Glamoc being bitter that the government organs had provided almost no help at all in evacuation and salvaging of property?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such discussions did not take place at all. A quarrel emerged as to who was responsible for the fall of these municipalities. There was a conflict, and that's where the discussions ended. We parted ways. And I really wondered at how this was possible. This was a conflict between Mladic and Karadzic and whatnot. It was an old affair. The Assembly meddled in that later on, or whether the Assembly meeting was before, I don't know. I didn't really study events. I can't testify to that. I can only testify to the fact that the meeting started and then all of a sudden somebody said, The aviation is striking, and we just fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please, and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The comment at the bottom of the page in English from this meeting says: "The people withdrew spontaneously, but quite successfully and without major casualties, taking part of their property and driving bovine cattle. They are particularly bitter about the fact that the government organs provided almost no help at all in the evacuation and salvaging of property." Does that refresh your recollection at all as to whether that was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see written here is not something that was the subject of discussions. Perhaps somebody wrote it down after the meeting or before the meeting. At any rate, it was not discussed at the meeting. We got in together and left together:

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Exhibit D1495, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who Rade Raseta was at that time? General, General, can you tell us who Rade Raseta was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Rade Raseta was chief of security. They rotated frequently. I'm not sure, but I think he was chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, what we have on the screen here is a report prepared on the 3rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And he's writing to Dimitrijevic, who is who? Tell the Court who Mr. Dimitrijevic is at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dimitrijevic was chief of the Security Administration of the Army of Yugoslavia, of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. He was -- we had Aco Vasiljevic, and this is Aleksandar Dimitrijevic. He was holding that position for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look down to the second paragraph, or I guess the middle of that one large paragraph, it says: "In the course of the day," this is 3 August, "the chief of the Krajina Serb Army General Staff established contact with the forward command post of the Serb Republic Army General Staff in regard of the joint operations and planning of further offensive operations along the Grahovo-Livno axis." Do you recall, the day before Operation Storm, establishing contact with the forward command post of the VRS General Staff concerning further offensive -- joint operations, further offensive operations along the Grahovo-Livno axis?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, because at the time Mladic went to Ostraj [phoen]. Before Mladic arrived, I was unable to establish any communication, perhaps. But it was a fait accompli. Nothing could be done anymore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the person the witness said he couldn't establish communication with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says here that artillery engaged in retaliation, this wasn't done. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the person you said you could not establish contact with.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Chief of Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Milovanovic. One could never know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page 4 of this document in English, which is the very end of the document in B/C/S under section 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say that this security officer added this in writing at his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, your chief or assistant chief of security is writing to the Yugoslav Army General Staff, Security Administration, on the 3rd of August, and he reports: "On 3 August 1995, I was in contact with the citizens, and I had the impression that there are certain elements of panic, yet still under control. The citizens mostly blame the government, that is, the state leadership of the Republic of the Serb Krajina. They believe that their neglect and irresponsibility caused the consequences we are faced with now. They hope that we have not been betrayed and abandoned and that, as the last possibility, the FRY will help. Furthermore, the citizens believe that we are not able to defend ourselves and that, should there be no significant help by the FRY, it would be better for the people to resettle to other areas rather than stay here to face encirclement and death."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't sign the document. What sort of policy was developed by security, I don't know. I didn't receive this document, and we did not have this situation. The situation that I know of was the one where prevailed -- where confidence prevailed. But I needed three more months. I never heard from this security officer, Raseta, or his assistants, or his subordinates, the KOS's counter-intelligence officers, that the population should move out. I suppose I should have been the first one to know this and not someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Misetic has read a part of a document to you. He has not even put a question to you. Nevertheless, you spent all right eight lines on giving comments. Why not wait what Mr. Misetic would like to know from you? Mr. Misetic, what would be your question in relation to this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, this document comes from your General Staff, by someone under your command, and I just wanted to ask you: Was it, in fact, the situation, as reported here --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. This assessment about the citizens believing that if -- "Believe that we are unable to defend ourselves and that, should there be no significant help by the FRY, it would be better for the people to resettle to other areas, rather than stay here to face encirclement and death." Was that your understanding of the situation among the citizens on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see, this was the opinion on the part of the Security Service, along their chain, which did not include mine. Whether their operatives knew more than I did is something I cannot say. I know the extent of what I know, and the information that I received through the chain of command was that there was readiness and preparedness to stay in the area and fight; however, that all steps should be taken to avert a war. The Assembly in Topusko asked me, as a commander, whether we were able to defend ourselves. I said that we were not able to defend ourselves and that we should look for other solutions, we should engage in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to Exhibit D923 again, please. Now, if we could first go to page 3 in the English, please. I'm sorry. Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page -- the bottom, it says, "page 21 of 29." It's page 21. It's page 13 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look, General --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is that report of the 26th of August. And I just wanted to ask you about this line. There is a sentence in here which talks about Western Slavonia right in the middle of the screen in English, and it says: "After the fall of Western Slavonia, there were many accusations at the expense of the authority, the president of the republic, because the evacuation was not ordered earlier." Now, do you recall, prior to Operation Storm, criticism of the authorities for not ordering the evacuation of the population of Western Slavonia earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about Western Slavonia. I came after Western Slavonia. There was no talk about Western Slavonia. I arrived there to heal the wounds of Western Slavonia, to change the climate. I didn't know about the reactions, the recriminations, the accusations. I think that they accused mostly Republika Srpska for failing to assist the people pulling out of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 now of this document in English, please. It's page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it says here: "The aggression was expected, and the Main Staff directed the main focus of their work on preparing the units to defend their positions, regions, and areas resolutely for five to seven days, believing that that would be enough for the international factors and, if necessary, even the Yugoslav Army, to react." Now, why was it part of your strategy to anticipate international factors and perhaps the Yugoslav Army reacting? What were you hoping the international factors would do?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were expecting the international factors to react because we were in a United Nations protected zone. That United Nations protected zone came under strike of the Croatian professional army, the entire army of 160.000 men, attacking unarmed people. We expected that nothing would happen, that the international community would be -- would have to be ashamed of. As regards the use of the Army of Yugoslavia, of the Yugoslav Army, this was said rather as more a boosting factor, to boost the morale of the soldiers, because we knew that they would not be used, that the Yugoslav Army would not -- you knew that the Yugoslav Army would not be used, as did I. We had such close cooperation ties that this was a known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even the East Slavonia Corps was used, which ostensibly was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would that be the 11th Corps ?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the East Slavonia Corps, which is the strongest corps. It was just looking on as we were suffering. We knew that the forces were being pulled in, that there would be an imminent attack, but nothing was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about the 11th Corps a little bit later. Okay? But let me turn your attention to Exhibit D389, please. Can you tell us who Mihajlo Knezevic was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some sort of a security or intelligence officer. A lieutenant-colonel was here, lieutenant-colonel, an intelligence officer. Yes, yes, that is what he was. He gathered intelligence on you, and his intelligence was quite precise. I mean, he gathered the intelligence on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Speaking of precise intelligence, let's look at this document. And if you look at the fourth paragraph, this is the report that he prepared on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Knin-Livanjsko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He reports, talking about the 4th of August, he says: "The first strike was carried out on the building of the SVK General Staff, which suffered great material damage with the fleet of vehicles almost completely destroyed. Later the fire was transferred on the military barracks, '1300 kaplar', the Tvik factory, the railway intersection, residential buildings in the area beneath the Knin fortress, et cetera." Now, that intelligence information from Mr. Knezevic on the 4th of August, is that consistent with your --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The railway hub is what matters. That is, of course, the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why does the railway's hub matter?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the railway hub -- this railway hub, it was the biggest one in this area of Croatia, the biggest traffic -- railway traffic intersection in the Knin area. I don't know why it was important and why it was shelled, because there was no railway traffic and the army was not using that hub. But as you are asking me about this paragraph and what is written here is correct, that -- I spent that night at the orders -- or, rather, the suggestion of my personal security guards in town, in a house of a commander, and they were guarding me there. When the bombing started, I sat in a vehicle with my security guards and left for the command post. En route, because of the heavy artillery shelling, we had to stop and take shelter in basements of residential houses, and there I saw people, women and children, with their hands on their ears. Women would be running out of houses naked, and they would ask me, General, what kind of an artillery shelling is this? We have shells coming in through the windows. And then I explained to them, These are rockets, not ordinary shells. And they whizzed with such a terrible sound as they landed, like we had in Belgrade. So now I arrive at the command post. Can I explain about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: The intelligence information contained in here, is that the intelligence information you were, in fact, receiving on the morning of the 4th, in terms of what was being struck?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I got information the minute I entered the staff, in the basement, the operations conference room which was in the basement, and the officer on duty immediately informed me that they had hit the command so -- with such precision that they had punctured all our vehicles. A guard in the compound, a guard in the vehicles was killed. And they said they had never seen such precision shelling. Now, they used the 152 MM Howitzers. They had to have had a GPS system and a target analysts group because it was so precise. I never asked these gentlemen here what it was they shelled us with. But they continued to shell me, not the town, and that is something which amazed me, because had they continued, they would have finished their job. They just opened that fire. Now, why they did so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, the question was simply whether this was the intelligence information you received, not who then went on to shell you. That's -- try to focus on the questions. And you have some time to consider it, because, Mr. Misetic, I need five minutes, and it's 20 minutes to 2.00, so I suggest that unless it would be very unsuitable for you, to already ask the witness to be excused for the day only. Mr. Mrksic, we will continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. I'll further discuss with the parties our time scheduling also in order to see to what extent we will be able to accommodate you, so that's still on our mind. Meanwhile, I instruct you that you should not speak about your testimony, whether already given or whether still to be given, with anyone, and that includes Mr. Domazet, because the substance of your testimony is not to be discussed. Another matter is your position as a witness. That is within the scope of what you can discuss with Mr. Domazet. Is that clear to you? And that's clear to Mr. Domazet as well, I take it? Yes, that's confirmed. Then, Madam Usher, could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I telephone my wife and my children to tell them that I'm well, without, of course, ever talking about the subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, the weather or whether you feel well, these are the kind of subjects you can discuss with others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm first addressing you. We're close to five hours now, four hours more to go. That is, for tomorrow, we usually take three and a half effective hours of examination. Could you give us any estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my hope to finish tomorrow. I'm now into the 4th of August, so hopefully most of my time will be spent on that tomorrow. There are some things after the 4th of August, but I will do my best to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the other parties give me any indication on how much time they'll need for --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As things stand at the moment, Your Honour, we don't have any questions at all for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my questioning, of course, will very much depends on what Mr. Misetic will be asking before me. But for the present circumstances, I could estimate one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One session, which is a little bit not a full one hour and a half, but close to that. Mr. Russo, my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. President, I'm estimating about a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A day. Well, then, I'm glad that I'll be able, tomorrow, to tell Mr. Mrksic that where the family visit -- the first family visit is planned for Wednesday afternoon, that there is a fair chance - of course, we do not know what re-examination will bring - that he would be even free to prepare for that family visit during the morning hours. If we would need part of Wednesday morning, then it takes a bit of time between concluding a session and being transported back. Since the visit is expected at 1.00, that would certainly not be the whole of Wednesday morning, but if the parties could endeavour - and of course the Chamber may have some questions as well - to not go beyond part of the Tuesday. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is our objective as well, but I do want to let you know that we will have the next witness here, ready to go, hopefully Monday, and so, if for some unforeseen reason, there needs to be more time to examine him, if the Court wishes to take that witness out of turn on Wednesday so that the witness -- this witness can spend time with his family and then come back the next day, after the visit is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the point is that for the Wednesday afternoon, visits are planned, but for the two following days full-day visits are planned. So that is good to know, that the next witness is stand-by, and I think next week Friday we have scheduled another matter anyhow. So, therefore, we'll have to consider that. But let's try to do our utmost best to finish somewhere during Tuesday morning. We will adjourn until tomorrow, Friday, the 19th of June, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
